summary.text: Take \(n=p=2\): at argument \(4\), the gcd-product and factorial-product are both \(96\), so \(a(4)=1\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_2(a(4))=0\). On the other hand, \(\sum_{i\ge0}\left\lfloor\lfloor2/2^i\rfloor/2\right\rfloor=1\), since only the \(i=0\) term is nonzero, giving the required contradiction.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the conjecture by taking
\[
n=2,\qquad p=2.
\]
These values satisfy the hypotheses: \(n\) is positive and \(p=2\) is prime.

Recall that
\[
a(N)=\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{1\le j,k\le N}\gcd(j,k)}
{\displaystyle\prod_{1\le k\le N}\bigl(\lfloor N/k\rfloor!\bigr)^k}.
\]
For the chosen values, the argument of \(a\) on the left-hand side of the conjecture is \(np=4\). We therefore calculate \(a(4)\) directly.

The gcds \(\gcd(j,k)\) for \(1\le j,k\le 4\) form the table
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\gcd(j,k)&k=1&k=2&k=3&k=4\\ \hline
j=1&1&1&1&1\\
j=2&1&2&1&2\\
j=3&1&1&3&1\\
j=4&1&2&1&4
\end{array}
\]
Thus the products of the four entries in the respective rows are
\[
1,\qquad 4,\qquad 3,\qquad 8.
\]
Consequently, the numerator in the definition of \(a(4)\) is
\[
\prod_{1\le j,k\le4}\gcd(j,k)=1\cdot4\cdot3\cdot8=96.
\]

For the denominator, consider the four values of \(k\) separately. They give
\[
\begin{aligned}
k=1 &: \quad \bigl(\lfloor4/1\rfloor!\bigr)^1=(4!)^1=24,\\
k=2 &: \quad \bigl(\lfloor4/2\rfloor!\bigr)^2=(2!)^2=4,\\
k=3 &: \quad \bigl(\lfloor4/3\rfloor!\bigr)^3=(1!)^3=1,\\
k=4 &: \quad \bigl(\lfloor4/4\rfloor!\bigr)^4=(1!)^4=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Their product is therefore
\[
\prod_{k=1}^4\bigl(\lfloor4/k\rfloor!\bigr)^k
=24\cdot4\cdot1\cdot1=96.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(4)=\frac{96}{96}=1.
\]
No positive power of \(2\) divides \(1\), so the exponent of \(2\) in the prime factorization of \(a(4)\) is
\[
\operatorname{ord}_2(a(2\cdot2))=\operatorname{ord}_2(a(4))
=\operatorname{ord}_2(1)=0.
\]

We now evaluate the right-hand side predicted by the conjecture. Since \(b(m)=\lfloor m/2\rfloor\), that side is
\[
\sum_{i\ge0} b\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{2}{2^i}\right\rfloor\right)
=
\sum_{i\ge0}
\left\lfloor
\frac{\left\lfloor2/2^i\right\rfloor}{2}
\right\rfloor.
\]
For \(i=0\), we have \(2^0=1\), and hence the term is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor2/1\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac22\right\rfloor=1.
\]
For \(i=1\), the term is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor2/2\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac12\right\rfloor=0.
\]
Finally, if \(i\ge2\), then \(2^i\ge4>2\). Thus
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{2}{2^i}\right\rfloor=0,
\]
and the corresponding summand is also zero. Therefore every term except the term at \(i=0\) vanishes, and the conjectured right-hand side equals
\[
1+0+0+\cdots=1.
\]

For the positive integer \(n=2\) and the prime \(p=2\), the two sides of the proposed identity are consequently
\[
\operatorname{ord}_2(a(np))=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sum_{i\ge0}
\left\lfloor
\frac{\left\lfloor n/2^i\right\rfloor}{2}
\right\rfloor=1.
\]
Since \(0\ne1\), the asserted identity fails for \((n,p)=(2,2)\). Hence the universal conjecture is false.
